subject: music
title: Hip-hop origins (c. 1973–1986): Bronx block parties, breakbeats, and the first records
dek: In August 1973 Clive Campbell extended breaks on two turntables in a Bronx rec room. For six years the form belonged to parks and community centres. In 1979 a studio group put a party on a 12-inch, radio played it, and the majors arrived. By 1986 Run-DMC and Def Jam had built a commercial blueprint. This lesson covers the Bronx scene, Jamaica's toasting lineage, the first records, and what happened before MTV renamed it rap.

thumb.alt: 1520 Sedgwick Avenue apartment building in the Bronx, a tall brick residential tower.

hero.alt: 1520 Sedgwick Avenue apartment building in the Bronx, with surrounding buildings and street.
hero.caption: 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, Morris Heights, the Bronx, photographed in July 2009. On 11 August 1973 Cindy Campbell organised a back-to-school party in the building's rec room; her brother Clive Campbell (DJ Kool Herc) worked two turntables and a mixer to extend the breaks in funk and soul records. The party is widely cited as hip-hop's foundation event. The brick is the address, not the only origin — parks, schools, and community centres across the Bronx hosted similar gatherings through the 1970s. The building was designated a New York City landmark in 2023.

honesty: Early hip-hop photographs from 1973–1979 are rare; many Bronx party and park pictures from the era are in private or unclear-copyright hands. Most artist publicity photographs from the late 1970s and early 1980s are still under commercial copyright. This lesson uses street and building photographs from the Bronx, Jamaica, Paris, and other cities, plus equipment and venue images, all captioned as what they are: places and objects, not portraits. Where a free-license portrait could not be verified, the lesson does without. All YouTube links point to official or Topic uploads; when official audio is unavailable the note explains what the link is. No AI images of people. No invented facts, quotes, or numbers.

timeline.label: Bronx fires, Jamaican sound systems, disco breaks
timeline.detail: The South Bronx in the late 1960s and early 1970s: urban renewal, highway construction, disinvestment, and fires leave whole blocks empty. Clive Campbell emigrates from Kingston, Jamaica, in 1967, bringing knowledge of sound-system culture and toasting (spoken vocals over instrumental tracks). In discos and at parties, dancers respond most strongly to the instrumental breaks in funk, soul, and Latin records — the sections where drums and bass are isolated. DJs notice.

timeline.label: Cindy Campbell's party, 1520 Sedgwick Avenue
timeline.detail: Cindy Campbell organises a back-to-school fundraiser party in the rec room of 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, Morris Heights. Her brother Clive Campbell, using the DJ name Kool Herc, plays two copies of the same record on two turntables, switching between them to loop the break — the percussive, vocal-free section dancers want. He calls the dancers break-boys and break-girls. Coke La Rock, a friend, takes the microphone and speaks rhythmically over the music. The method spreads.

timeline.label: Parks, rec centres, and the scene vocabulary
timeline.detail: The breakbeat technique moves into Bronx parks — Cedar Park, PS 63 schoolyard, Webster Avenue PAL — and other rec rooms. DJ Kool Herc, Afrika Bambaataa (who founds the Zulu Nation in 1973), and Grandmaster Flash refine the art. Flash develops cutting and backspinning to make breaks seamless. MCs (masters of ceremonies) — Coke La Rock, Melle Mel, Cowboy, Busy Bee Starski — develop spoken routines over the beats. Breakdancing (B-boying) becomes a parallel practice. Graffiti writers and breakers share crews. No records yet; this is a live, local culture.

timeline.label: The first commercial rap record
timeline.detail: On 16 September 1979 the Sugarhill Gang — Big Bank Hank, Wonder Mike, and Master Gee, assembled by Sylvia Robinson — release "Rapper's Delight" on Sugar Hill Records. The 15-minute 12-inch uses a live band replaying Chic's "Good Times" and studio rappers, not the established Bronx MCs. It reaches number 36 on the Billboard Hot 100 and sells millions. Many Bronx pioneers resent the record for packaging a park culture into a commercial product without crediting them, but "Rapper's Delight" proves rap can be pressed and sold.

timeline.label: More records, more labels, and "The Message"
timeline.detail: Kurtis Blow releases "The Breaks" (Mercury, 1980), the first rap single on a major label and the first certified gold rap record. Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five sign to Sugar Hill. In 1982 they release "The Message," written largely by Duke Bootee and Melle Mel, a social-commentary track about poverty and urban decay. The same year Afrika Bambaataa and Soulsonic Force release "Planet Rock" (Tommy Boy), fusing the Roland TR-808 drum machine with Kraftwerk's "Trans-Europe Express" to create electro-funk. These records move hip-hop from breakbeats into synthesised production.

timeline.label: Def Jam, Run-DMC, and the crossover
timeline.detail: Russell Simmons and Rick Rubin found Def Jam Recordings in 1984. Run-DMC — Joseph Simmons (Run), Darryl McDaniels (DMC), and Jason Mizell (Jam Master Jay) — release their debut album in 1984 and Raising Hell in 1986. "Walk This Way," a collaboration with Aerosmith, brings rap to rock radio and MTV. Def Jam signs LL Cool J and the Beastie Boys. By 1986 the independent Bronx party has become a commercial format on major labels. This lesson stops here; the golden age and gangsta-rap eras belong to later capsules.

fun_fact.title: 1520 Sedgwick Avenue was designated a New York City landmark in 2023, fifty years after the party
fun_fact.text: On 9 May 2023 the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission designated 1520 Sedgwick Avenue as an individual landmark, marking its role in the birth of hip-hop. The rec room where Cindy Campbell held the August 1973 party no longer exists in its original form — the building has been renovated several times — but the address remains a pilgrimage site. In 2007 it was recognised by the New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation as the birthplace of hip-hop. The designation protects the building's exterior from demolition or significant alteration. Clive Campbell (DJ Kool Herc) attended the 2023 ceremony.

sections.title: The Bronx after the fires, Jamaica's sound systems, and the breaks dancers wanted

blocks.text: The South Bronx in the late 1960s and early 1970s was a borough under pressure. Robert Moses's Cross Bronx Expressway, completed in stages from 1948 to 1972, had cut through dense residential neighbourhoods. Urban renewal and highway construction displaced thousands of families. White flight, redlining, and landlord arson — burning buildings to collect insurance — left blocks of rubble. By 1973 the South Bronx was a national image of urban collapse. The people who stayed needed cheap recreation. Block parties, park jams, and rec-room gatherings filled the gap.

Clive Campbell was born in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1955 and emigrated with his family to the Bronx in 1967. In Kingston he had witnessed sound-system culture: mobile discos with enormous speaker stacks, DJs who selected records, and toasters who spoke or chanted over instrumental B-sides. Toasting — rhythmic speech over music — was already an established Jamaican form by the time Campbell left. Artists like U-Roy, Dennis Alcapone, and Big Youth were recording toasted tracks for producers like Duke Reid and Coxsone Dodd. Campbell carried that knowledge to New York, where disco DJs were playing Motown, funk, and soul for dancers who wanted the beat.

Dancers responded most strongly to the break: the moment in a funk or soul record when the vocals dropped out and the drums, bass, and percussion were isolated. James Brown's "Give It Up or Turnit a Loose," the Incredible Bongo Band's "Apache," and Babe Ruth's "The Mexican" had breaks that made people move. DJs noticed that when the break played, the floor filled. But breaks lasted only seconds. The question was how to make them last longer. Clive Campbell worked out the answer in his family's apartment in the Bronx, using two copies of the same record, two turntables, and a mixer.

sections.title: 11 August 1973: Cindy Campbell's party and the breakbeat loop

blocks.text: On 11 August 1973 Cindy Campbell, Clive Campbell's sister, organised a back-to-school party in the rec room of 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, Morris Heights, the Bronx. She needed money for new clothes; she charged admission. Clive, who had started calling himself DJ Kool Herc, brought his sound system — two Shure columns and a pair of Thorens or Technics turntables — and played records. The method he used that night was the one he had been developing at home: he played two copies of the same record on two turntables, cueing one to the start of the break while the other played, then switching at the last second to loop the break indefinitely. He called the technique the Merry-Go-Round. He called the dancers who responded break-boys and break-girls.

Coke La Rock, a friend of Herc's, took the microphone and began speaking over the music: shouting out the names of people in the room, hyping the crowd, punctuating the beat with phrases. This was not singing. It was rhythmic speech, closer to Jamaican toasting than to American radio DJ patter. The combination of the extended break and the spoken-word hype created a new format: the music was a loop, the DJ was the architect, and the MC was the voice on top. This is the party that historians and practitioners most often cite as hip-hop's foundation.

The event was not unique. Other DJs in the Bronx — Grandmaster Flowers, Pete DJ Jones — were also playing for dancers and extending breaks, though their techniques varied. What made the Sedgwick party important was that Kool Herc's method worked and spread. He began playing at other venues: the Twilight Zone on Jerome Avenue, the Hevalo Club on 183rd Street, and Cedar Park in Sedgwick. Word travelled. Other DJs copied the technique. By 1974 Herc had a crew: Coke La Rock and Clark Kent on the mics, and a sound system loud enough to fill parks. This was still a live culture. No one was recording yet.

sections.title: Parks, rec centres, crews, and the vocabulary that stuck

blocks.text: Between 1974 and 1978 the breakbeat party moved from rec rooms into parks and schoolyards. DJ Kool Herc played Cedar Park (University Avenue and Sedgwick Avenue), the Webster PAL (Police Athletic League), and the Hevalo. Afrika Bambaataa, a former member of the Black Spades street gang, founded the Universal Zulu Nation in 1973 as a community organisation and began DJing at the Bronx River Community Center. Grandmaster Flash — Joseph Saddler, born in Barbados, raised in the Bronx — refined the technical side. He developed cutting (moving between records without losing the beat) and backspinning (spinning the record backward to reset the break instantly). Flash's sound system was quieter than Herc's but more precise. By the late 1970s Flash, Herc, and Bambaataa were recognised as the Bronx's three DJ pioneers, each with a separate following.

The microphone work evolved from shouting names into structured routines. The term "MC" (master of ceremonies) stuck; "rapper" came later. Coke La Rock and Clark Kent worked with Herc. Melle Mel (Melvin Glover), Cowboy (Keith Wiggins), Scorpio (Eddie Morris), Rahiem (Guy Williams), and Kidd Creole (Nathaniel Glover) joined Grandmaster Flash as the Furious Five. Busy Bee Starski and Kurtis Blow performed at multiple venues. The MCs traded boasts, announced the DJ, and kept the crowd engaged. This was not yet singing or verse-chorus structure. It was call-and-response over an endless loop.

Breakdancing and graffiti ran parallel. Break-boys and break-girls developed acrobatic floor moves during the breaks: spins, freezes, and footwork. Graffiti writers tagged subway cars and walls, creating a visual vocabulary for the same youth culture. Crews formed around all three practices — DJing, MCing, and breaking. The Rock Steady Crew, founded by Jimmy D and Jojo in 1977, became the most recognised breaking crew. The whole cluster — DJs, MCs, breakers, and writers — shared venues, parties, and a name. By the late 1970s the Bronx press and the early hip-hop practitioners themselves were calling it hip-hop, a term some credit to Lovebug Starski or Keith Cowboy, though the origin is disputed.

blocks.alt: The Cross Bronx Expressway elevated structure with residential buildings in the background.
blocks.caption: The Cross Bronx Expressway, photographed in 2008. The highway, completed in stages from 1948 to 1972, cut through dense Bronx neighbourhoods and displaced thousands of families. The elevated structure and the residential blocks behind it show the urban geography where hip-hop emerged in the 1970s.

sections.title: 1979: "Rapper's Delight" and the studio version of a park party

blocks.text: For six years hip-hop existed as a live event. The Bronx DJs and MCs did not record because the equipment was expensive, the music was made from other people's records (sampling was not yet legally settled), and no label saw a market. Sylvia Robinson changed that. Robinson was a singer and producer who had recorded "Love Is Strange" with Mickey & Sylvia in 1956 and "Pillow Talk" as a solo artist in 1973. In 1979 she co-founded Sugar Hill Records with her husband Joe Robinson and decided to record a rap single. She assembled a studio group — Big Bank Hank (Henry Jackson), Wonder Mike (Michael Wright), and Master Gee (Guy O'Brien) — who had little connection to the established Bronx scene. They rapped over a live band's replay of Chic's "Good Times." The track ran 15 minutes and was pressed as a 12-inch single.

"Rapper's Delight" was released on 16 September 1979. It reached number 36 on the Billboard Hot 100 and sold millions of copies internationally. It introduced rap to radio programmers and record buyers who had never heard of Kool Herc or Grandmaster Flash. Many Bronx pioneers resented the record. Big Bank Hank had borrowed lines from Grandmaster Caz (Curtis Brown) of the Cold Crush Brothers without credit. The live-band approach erased the DJ. The three rappers were studio hires, not battle-tested MCs. The record packaged and commercialised a culture that had been local, collective, and unrecorded. But "Rapper's Delight" proved rap could be sold. Labels followed.

Kurtis Blow (Kurt Walker) released "The Breaks" on Mercury in 1980, the first rap single on a major label and the first certified gold rap record. Mercury's distribution gave the record national reach. Blow performed on Soul Train, proving rap could work on television. The same year Grandmaster Flash signed to Sugar Hill and began recording with the Furious Five. In October 1981 Flash released "The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash on the Wheels of Steel," a seven-minute live-mixed turntable track that demonstrated cutting, scratching, and backspin on record. This was closer to what a Bronx DJ actually did than "Rapper's Delight" had been.

sections.title: "The Message" and "Planet Rock": social commentary and synthesisers

blocks.text: On 1 July 1982 Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five released "The Message" on Sugar Hill. The track was written mostly by Ed "Duke Bootee" Fletcher and Melle Mel; Flash and the other members of the Furious Five did not perform on it. The lyrics described poverty, crime, and urban decay: "Broken glass everywhere / People pissing on the stairs, you know they just don't care." This was not party music. It was social commentary. "The Message" reached number 62 on the Hot 100 and became one of the most-cited rap records of all time. It showed that rap could carry narrative and politics, not just boasts and rhythm.

Five months earlier, in March 1982, Afrika Bambaataa and Soulsonic Force (Mr. Biggs, Pow Wow, and G.L.O.B.E.) had released "Planet Rock" on Tommy Boy Records. Bambaataa and producer Arthur Baker used the Roland TR-808 drum machine and sampled Kraftwerk's "Trans-Europe Express" and "Numbers," layering electronic synth lines over a rigid 808 kick. The result was electro-funk: mechanical, synthetic, futuristic. "Planet Rock" became a dance-floor standard and influenced the development of techno and Miami bass. It marked the moment when hip-hop stopped being only about breakbeats from funk records and started building its own electronic sound.

By 1982 hip-hop had three commercial directions: party rap (Sugarhill Gang, Kurtis Blow), social commentary (The Message), and electronic production (Planet Rock). These were not yet genres. They were early records that showed rap could do more than one thing. The Bronx scene continued in parks and clubs, but the centre of gravity was shifting toward record deals, radio play, and MTV.

blocks.alt: A Roland TR-808 drum machine, a grey metal box with black and red buttons and knobs.
blocks.caption: A Roland TR-808 drum machine photographed in 2005. The TR-808, released in 1980 and discontinued in 1983, became the defining instrument of electro-funk and later hip-hop. Afrika Bambaataa used it on "Planet Rock" (1982); its bass kick and snare became signatures of 1980s rap production.

sections.title: Def Jam, Run-DMC, and the major-label crossover

blocks.text: Russell Simmons managed Kurtis Blow and Run-DMC; Rick Rubin was a white New York University student who produced records in his dorm room. In 1984 they founded Def Jam Recordings and distributed through Columbia Records. The label's aesthetic was harder and sparser than Sugar Hill's: no live bands, no disco polish, just drum machines, samples, and aggressive vocals. LL Cool J (James Todd Smith) was 16 when he sent Rubin a demo tape; his debut album Radio (1985) became Def Jam's first gold record. The Beastie Boys, a white punk-turned-rap group, signed to Def Jam and released Licensed to Ill in 1986, the first rap album to reach number one on the Billboard 200.

Run-DMC — Joseph Simmons (Run), Darryl McDaniels (DMC), and Jason Mizell (Jam Master Jay) — were Russell Simmons's flagship group. Their self-titled debut in 1984 and King of Rock in 1985 used minimal production: drum machines, scratch samples, and hard vocal delivery. In 1986 they released Raising Hell on Profile Records. The album included "Walk This Way," a collaboration with Aerosmith that merged rap with rock guitar. The music video, directed by Jon Small, showed Run-DMC and Aerosmith breaking through a wall to perform together. MTV played it in heavy rotation. The single reached number four on the Hot 100. The album sold three million copies. "Walk This Way" opened rock radio to rap and brought rap to white suburban audiences who had ignored the Sugarhill Gang.

By 1986 hip-hop was no longer a Bronx secret. It had labels, distribution, MTV presence, and major-label deals. Run-DMC performed at Madison Square Garden. The Beastie Boys toured with Madonna. Def Jam was generating millions of dollars. The independent party Kool Herc had invented in 1973 had become a commercial format. This is where this lesson stops. The golden age (1987–1992), gangsta rap, West Coast production, and the East Coast–West Coast split belong to later capsules. The foundation — the breakbeat, the MC, the DJ, the 808, and the first commercial blueprint — was laid in the Bronx between 1973 and 1986.

sections.title: Jamaica's toasting lineage and contemporaneous scenes in Paris, London, and Sydney

blocks.text: Hip-hop did not invent rhythmic speech over music. That form came from Jamaica. In Kingston in the 1960s and 1970s, sound-system DJs like U-Roy, Big Youth, Dennis Alcapone, and I-Roy spoke and chanted over instrumental reggae and dub tracks. This was called toasting. The practice had roots in Jamaican radio DJs like Count Machuki in the 1950s. Producers like Coxsone Dodd (Studio One) and Duke Reid (Treasure Isle) pressed toasted tracks onto B-sides and, later, as full singles. By the early 1970s toasting was a commercial reggae subgenre. When Clive Campbell emigrated from Kingston to the Bronx in 1967, he brought that knowledge. The breakbeat loop was his innovation; the spoken vocal was a Jamaican inheritance.

blocks.alt: A painted blue building in downtown Kingston, Jamaica.
blocks.caption: A painted building in downtown Kingston, Jamaica, photographed in 2017. Kingston's sound-system culture in the 1960s–1970s — mobile discos with enormous speakers, DJs selecting records, and toasters chanting over instrumental dub — provided the template for the Bronx's spoken-word-over-beats format. Clive Campbell (DJ Kool Herc) carried that knowledge to New York in 1967.
blocks.credit: Ralf Steinberger / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 2.0

blocks.text: In Paris hip-hop arrived in the early 1980s through radio and imports. Sidney Duteil's H.I.P. H.O.P. show on Radio 7 (later Radio Nova) played New York records starting in 1980. French youth began breaking, DJing, and rapping in French. Dee Nasty (Daniel Bigeault) released the first French rap record, "Paname City Rappin'," in 1984. By the mid-1980s groups like NTM (Suprême NTM) and IAM were forming. The Paris banlieues (suburbs) became centres for French hip-hop, with social conditions—housing projects, unemployment, racial segregation—that paralleled the South Bronx. French hip-hop was contemporaneous with the Bronx's commercial phase, not derivative: it used the same tools (turntables, drum machines, microphones) to address local conditions.

blocks.alt: Sarcelles housing estate with apartment towers.
blocks.caption: Sarcelles, a banlieue north of Paris, showing the housing estate towers. In the early 1980s French youth in the suburbs of Paris and other cities adopted breakdancing, DJing, and rapping. Dee Nasty released the first French rap record in 1984. The banlieues, like the South Bronx, were sites of social housing, unemployment, and disinvestment — parallel urban conditions that made hip-hop's language portable.

blocks.text: In London electro and hip-hop intersected with sound-system culture in Afro-Caribbean communities. Malcolm McLaren's "Buffalo Gals" (1982) brought scratching and breakbeat to British pop. Street Sounds Electro, a compilation series launched in 1983, introduced British audiences to New York electro. Breakdancing appeared in British cities in 1983–1984. By the mid-1980s British MCs were rapping over reggae and electro beats; this evolved into jungle, drum and bass, and grime in later decades. The early moment—1982–1986—was one of import and imitation, with British youth adapting New York forms to British accents and sound-system infrastructure.

In Sydney breakdancing and graffiti arrived in 1983–1984 through films like Wild Style (1983) and Beat Street (1984) and through TV broadcasts. Australian youth formed breaking crews and DJ crews in the western suburbs of Sydney. Sound Unlimited, an Australian hip-hop group, formed in 1983 and released early tracks in the mid-1980s. The scene was small and scattered, but it existed. The point is not that Sydney invented hip-hop. The point is that the form—two turntables, a microphone, a breakbeat, and a voice—could be copied and adapted anywhere young people had access to records, radio, and film. By 1986 hip-hop was a transnational format.

sections.title: MTV, major labels, and the next commercial chapters

blocks.text: In 1988 MTV launched Yo! MTV Raps, hosted by Fab 5 Freddy (Fred Brathwaite) in New York and Ed Lover and Doctor Dré (André Brown) in Los Angeles. The show brought rap videos into American living rooms daily and made hip-hop a mass-market format. Public Enemy's It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back (Def Jam, 1988), N.W.A's Straight Outta Compton (Ruthless, 1988), and De La Soul's 3 Feet High and Rising (Tommy Boy, 1989) represent the late-1980s explosion. By the early 1990s rap outsold rock in some American markets.

The golden age (roughly 1987–1993)—A Tribe Called Quest, Gang Starr, Eric B. & Rakim, the Native Tongues collective—emphasised lyrical complexity and jazz-sample production. Gangsta rap—N.W.A, Ice-T, later 2Pac and The Notorious B.I.G.—emphasised street narratives and West Coast G-funk. Both strands outgrew the 1973–1986 foundation this lesson covers. By the mid-1990s hip-hop was the subject of Congressional hearings, moral panic, and billion-dollar major-label catalogues. The Bronx party had become an industry.

What remains from 1973–1986 is the blueprint: two turntables and a mixer (Kool Herc), the DJ as architect (Grandmaster Flash), the MC as voice (Melle Mel, Kurtis Blow, Run-DMC), the 808 as drum section (Afrika Bambaataa), and the commercial structure (Sugar Hill, Def Jam). Later producers, MCs, and labels built on that blueprint, but they did not invent it. The invention happened in the Bronx, in rec rooms and parks, between 1973 and 1979, before anyone pressed a record. The next music capsules can take the golden age, the West Coast, or trap. This one stops when hip-hop left the park and entered the industry.

If hip-hop began as a local, unrecorded party culture in the Bronx, and became a billion-dollar global industry within 20 years, what parts of the original practice survived the commercial transition, and what parts were left behind in the parks?
